raw: [L0031] A reference oracle certifies AGREEMENT, not correctness — and only over the surface the reference actually SPANS | tier: canonical | added: 2026-08-10 | consolidated: 2026-08-11 | tags: oracles, testing, parity, coverage, architecture, doctrine, cross-project, HIGH-PRIORITY | lesson: parity-to-a-reference is the strongest available check on FIDELITY and is blind in TWO distinct ways, both of which present as a large green suite. (A) IT SHARES THE REFERENCE'S BUGS — it answers "does the port match the sketch?", never "is the sketch right?", so a defect present in both is not merely missed, it is CERTIFIED, and every passing scenario increases confidence in it. (B) IT COVERS ONLY THE SURFACE THE REFERENCE RENDERS, and there are three recurring ways to fall outside that surface: (1) THE SHELL PATH — an oracle that constructs the core DIRECTLY never exercises the integration layer, so a shell-side default divergence is invisible; before letting a new param SHARE an existing shell id, check whether ANY oracle drives the shell->core path at that param's default, and if not, give the second engine its own param with its own reference default so the goldens AND the shipped plugin are reference-exact by construction. (2) THE SUPERSET — a deliberate implementation-only range the reference does not implement is invisible BY CONSTRUCTION; parity passes forever while the superset region does anything at all, so the same commit that ADDS a superset must add an invariant oracle for it. (3) THE LAYER — anything downstream of what the reference renders gets ZERO coverage, and the green is seductive precisely because it is large and unrelated; before offering a passing fidelity suite as evidence for a change, state which layer the reference renders and whether the change is inside it. Three consequences: (i) oracles come in KINDS and a project needs more than one — fidelity (parity/golden), invariant (property checks needing no reference), closed-form; (ii) an invariant oracle outlives the reference and is the most donatable artifact across projects ([[L0030]]); (iii) THE REFERENCE IS A STAGE, NOT A FIXTURE — a prototype-as-spec is a scaffold with a ceiling, and the graduation path is toward references with an independent claim to truth (a high-accuracy integrator, a closed form, a measurement). | evidence: HYPERSAW, four independent instances. (A) consonance gravity integrated once per render call at dt = block length, so output depended on how a buffer was SUBDIVIDED; 147 parity scenarios passed for the entire life of that bug and COULD NOT have failed, since generator and checker both render at a fixed block. A ~40-line property check found it on first run, then found pan motion immediately after (ADR-086, tools/subdiv_check.cpp). (B1) ADR-055: spectra_check builds SpectraCore directly, so sharing the SAW ADSR ids would have pushed SAW's 0.003 s default into an engine whose reference wants 0.004 s — goldens green, shipped plugin diverged; own params 65-68 chosen instead. (B2) ADR-025 super-width: width > 1 is implementation-only, and its negative cross-feed injected phase-inverted saws — 0 cliffs at width <= 1.01, 1414 at width 1.5 — denied repeatedly by me because every check was structurally blind (JS clamps by construction; goldens and waveshape_check all ran width <= 1). The human isolated it by settings-bisection. (B3) 2026-08-11: the 147 goldens render SwarmCore directly, so the whole plugin mix stage (bass-mono, FX rack, master volume) is downstream of them; replacing rack.processStereo with the routing matrix would have shown 147/147 green whether bit-exact or catastrophically wrong, and the actual proof was routing_check assertion 8 (0/1024 samples differ, four active distinct slots). entry.evidence: HYPERSAW 2026-08-09/10 — mixer_check (tritone rewrite), the abandoned oscdrift probe, subdiv_check's first calibration, and the sample-rate probe that then found a real +0.42% defect once corrected.
entry.falsifier: a probe whose zero-control passed while the probe itself was still confounded — which would mean the control shared the confound too, and is the reason a control must be chosen to be independent of the mechanism under test rather than merely convenient.
entry.lesson: the dangerous measurement is not the one that fails, it is the one that AGREES WITH YOUR HYPOTHESIS for a reason unrelated to the hypothesis. Four instances in a single day, each a different mechanism, each producing a plausible number in the predicted direction: (1) a mute probe separated two oscillators by an OCTAVE, so oscillator 1's second harmonic landed on oscillator 2's fundamental and muting read as a 67% leak — the detector's frequency choice shared the signal's harmonic structure; (2) an oscillator-drift probe captured one oscillator 70 blocks after the other, comparing two MOMENTS of an evolving swarm rather than two oscillators — the detector's timing shared the system's evolution; (3) a gate calibration planted its regression with an unasserted string replace that matched nothing, so "the gate passed" was read as evidence when nothing had been planted — the plant shared the silent-no-op failure mode it was testing for; (4) a sample-rate invariance probe sampled every 256 SAMPLES, so its own time resolution tracked the sample rate, manufacturing a 1.4% variation that vanished when resolution was equalised in TIME — the detector's resolution shared the variable under test. THE CONTROL IS THE CURE: include a case that must read EXACTLY zero, and make the probe report it. WHEN THE SUBJECT IS A REPORT RATHER THAN A SIGNAL, the control must be negative: a diagnostic dump is a text file full of plausible-looking lines, and 'the value appears in the file' is satisfied by a file that mentions every value — so each positive assertion pairs with one that must NOT match, on a capture taken from a state where the thing genuinely is absent. That reshaped a real oracle: 'the gated voice is visible' only became meaningful once paired with 'and after release, none' (tools/trace_check.cpp, 2026-08-11). A gravity-off render differing by 0 of 132,300 samples is what proved the rig contributed nothing; the same control, run first, is what exposed (2) by "failing" at 0.84 with nothing to fail about. Corollary for tooling: every mutation in a calibration asserts its anchor, because a plant that silently does nothing and a fix that silently works are indistinguishable from the outside. NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT, learned 2026-08-11 by watching a second plant report the FIRST plant's failures verbatim: **asserting the anchor proves the SOURCE changed, never that the BINARY did.** A stale object file makes the calibration measure the previous experiment, and it presents as the most convincing possible result — a plant that 'fires' exactly as predicted. Force the rebuild (delete the object, not just re-run the build system, which may not track a header or a sibling translation unit as a dependency of the test target). Third occurrence of the stale-object half in three different tools. Corollary of the corollary: a plant whose failure is IDENTICAL to the previous plant's, including assertions it should not touch, is a stale binary until proven otherwise — the discriminator is an assertion the new plant CANNOT affect.

entry.evidence: two independent instances in `tools/routing_check.cpp`. (1) increment 1: the routing lab's terminal-test bug was a no-op because `isTerminal` excludes illegal destinations by its loop bound, not by the legality call — the protection is structural, and claiming the call provided it would have been a comment that lies. (2) increment 2 (2026-08-11): removing the `isTerminal` filter from the terminal sum was a no-op for the new bit-exactness assertion, because `setSerialChain` leaves `outAmount = 0` on non-terminals so summing them adds zeros — that assertion covers gather and aliasing (both plants fired, 1023/1024) but NOT terminal detection, which assertion 4 covers.
entry.falsifier: a no-op plant that, on inspection, is genuinely unreachable in any configuration rather than uncovered — then it is noise about the plant, not information about the assertion.
entry.lesson: when you plant a defect to prove an assertion is live and the suite stays GREEN, you have just measured the assertion's COVERAGE BOUNDARY — record it in the source next to the assertion, and do not silently retry with other plants until one fires. The instinct to keep trying is the bug: it converts "I discovered this assertion doesn't check X" into "I eventually found a plant that works", and the boundary is lost. Name explicitly which assertion DOES cover the thing the no-op plant probed, so the division is recorded rather than left to be assumed the other way.

entry.evidence: HYPERSAW, two NOTE_END bugs a year apart, both invisible to a full green suite because the AUDIO was correct in both. (1) 2026-08-03 (L0022): `emitNoteEnds` ignored `try_push`'s return and retired the tag anyway, so a busy host destroyed an END permanently — four rounds of wrong fixes chasing a stuck note before a REJECTING stub in the harness caught it. (2) 2026-08-11: `panicWithDump` zeroed `pendingEndCount` and cleared every tag, destroying every owed END; all EIGHTEEN gates green, the notes audibly stop, only the host's `note_id` bookkeeping is corrupted. It surfaced solely because an external reviewer asked which END cases were unmodeled and answering honestly required reading the function. Neither was findable by listening.
entry.falsifier: a project whose product-side oracles DO catch an obligation defect — which happens when the consumer's state feeds back into the product (a host that withholds retriggering a leaked pitch, as this one eventually did), so the corruption becomes audible downstream. The rule binds wherever the obligation surface is write-only from the producer's side.
entry.lesson: a system that both PRODUCES something and OWES a consumer bookkeeping about it has two observable surfaces, and an oracle suite usually covers only the first. Every check that measures the product — audio, rendered pixels, returned rows — stays green while the obligation surface is corrupted, because the product genuinely IS correct. The failure is invisible in the strongest sense: not merely unmeasured, but unmeasurable by the kind of test the project is full of, and it reaches the consumer as state corruption with no local symptom at all. Ask directly: what does this system PROMISE its consumer beyond the artifact — lifecycle events, acknowledgements, resource release, cleanup callbacks, transactional commits — and is any of it asserted? Every path that can DISCARD an obligation is the specific thing to enumerate; a system with two ways to drop an obligation, one that discharges it and one that does not, will eventually take the second. The structural cure is to make the discharging path the ONLY route (an identity that can leave only through the call that emits its end), so the defect has no spelling.

entry.evidence: independently arrived at in two repos within days, which is what promoted it. HYPERSAW: L0033's no-op calibration plants — a plant that does not fire measures a coverage boundary, recorded next to the assertion instead of retried until something fires; and `isTerminal()` computed rather than declared, so a manifest must NOT offer an `is_output` field or it becomes a second source of truth for a question the edges answer. FOUNDATIONS (2026-08-12, their DECISIONS #60/#61): a static_assert pinning that a model-A -> model-B -> model-A table PASSES validation, precisely so a later session cannot "fix" the validator into pre-ruling an open human question about feedback semantics; and a NoteTable with deliberately no clear()/reset()/panic(), so that a note identity cannot leave the table except through a path that delivers its END. Their framing of the convergence: two repos independently reaching "pin your refusals".
entry.falsifier: a deliberate absence that stayed absent across substantial refactoring by people who never saw the rationale — then prose sufficed and the test was ceremony. Note the asymmetry that makes this cheap: the test costs one assertion, and the failure it prevents is silent, plausible, and discovered late.
entry.lesson: systems record what they decided and almost never record what they deliberately did NOT decide. An omission with no assertion behind it is indistinguishable from an oversight, so the next competent person closes it — helpfully, plausibly, and wrongly. Whenever you leave something out ON PURPOSE (a capability withheld, a question left open for a human, a coverage boundary you found rather than closed), write the test that FAILS if someone adds it back. Three shapes recur: (1) a deliberately ABSENT operation — assert that no route to the forbidden state exists, so the absence is structural rather than remembered; (2) a deliberately UNANSWERED question — assert that the currently-illegal-looking case still VALIDATES, so nobody "fixes" the checker into pre-ruling it; (3) a deliberately UNCOVERED region — record the boundary next to the assertion that stops short of it, naming which other assertion does cover it. The general form: documentation of an intention is not enforcement of it, and an intention that only lives in prose is one refactor from being reversed by someone who never read the prose.
entry.supersedes_note: (generalises the discipline in [[L0033]], which stays as the calibration case)

entry.evidence: 2026-08-11, Place. `test/oracle/layer0.test.ts` "determinism (D5)" rendered twice and compared to itself; 27 tests green. Added `test/oracle/golden.test.ts` + `test/golden/goldens.json` (329 committed values, D16), inputs frozen under `fixtures/frozen/`. Five mutations each confirmed red then reverted: a Catmull-Rom `0.5*` → `0.5000001*` moved all 7 render hashes; `cloudToCutoffHz` 400→410; the submerged threshold `s < 0` → `s < -1` (surfaced via `waterFraction` 0.5143→0.5048); the D14 ramp-and-hold knee `2*(1-m)` → `2.1*(1-m)` (interior lens mixes only, endpoints correctly unaffected); dropping the tide `find(name==='M2') ??` fallback (caught on Galveston, a diurnal station where K1 outranks M2). A sixth attempt looked like a coverage gap but had substituted into a *comment* — the real predicate was `if (s < 0)`, and the corrected mutation failed as expected.
entry.falsifier: a render-path edit that changes output is caught by the two-renders-in-one-process determinism test with no committed expected value present.
entry.lesson: "Render the same request twice, assert the outputs are bit-identical" is the natural way to write a determinism oracle, and it is a **tautology under change**: both renders come from the same code, so any edit to the render path moves both together and the assertion stays green. It catches only genuine nondeterminism *within* a run (unseeded RNG, wall-clock reads, iteration-order dependence) — which is worth having, but it is not the property a reproducibility claim actually needs. That property is agreement with the **past**, and it requires an outside witness: an expected value committed *before* the change, which the change has to answer to. Two consequences worth internalizing. (1) The gap is invisible in a green suite and hides behind confident prose — here the roadmap named "committed golden render hashes" as the portable spec for a future plugin port in two places, and no such hash existed anywhere in the repo; `grep` for the hash format found nothing. When a doc asserts an artifact exists, grep for the artifact. (2) Split the comparison regime along whatever boundary the architecture already has, rather than picking one tolerance globally: where bit-exactness IS the product claim, compare exactly and let a cross-machine failure be loud information; where values only need to be behaviourally stable, compare to a relative tolerance, because `Math.pow`/`sin`/`atan2` are not required by IEEE-754 to be correctly rounded and demanding bit-equality on them fails across engines for reasons that are not regressions. Finally: **mutation-test the goldens before trusting them.** Perturb a constant in each covered path and confirm red. A golden suite never observed failing is decoration, and the check is cheap — it also catches the case where your own mutation silently hit a comment instead of code and you mistake a no-op for a coverage gap.

entry.evidence: plainsynth's `.claude/hooks/pretool-deny.sh` was ported from FOUNDATIONS' copy at spin-up (2026-08-12) to inherit its hard-won fixes — per-segment argument parsing, heredoc stripping, force-push flag placement, each of which had cost a real false positive or a real hole there. One block did not apply: FOUNDATIONS refuses broad stages (`git add -A`) because a CONSUMER may file into its `integrations/<name>/` mailbox mid-command, a race PreToolUse structurally cannot see. plainsynth is a pure consumer with no inbound mailbox, so the hazard cannot occur. It was dropped and replaced in-place with a `# --- NOT PORTED:` block stating the hazard, why it is impossible here, and the re-add trigger ("the moment this repo acquires an `integrations/<someone>/` directory another project's residents may write to"). Recorded in DECISIONS #3.
entry.falsifier: The failure mode here is PREDICTED, not yet observed — no session has yet mis-handled a silent divergence in this fleet. This entry is wrong if a shared guard diverges silently between two repos and a later session reconciles it correctly anyway (from git history, from the DECISIONS log, or by re-deriving the hazard), showing the in-code note was ceremony. It is also wrong if the notes themselves rot — if a `NOT PORTED` block's re-add trigger is observed to go stale and mislead a session more than the bare absence would have, the practice is a net negative and should be replaced by "diverge freely, reconcile from the source repo on demand".
entry.lesson: When harness code (a hook, a gate, a lint) is copied between sibling repos, some of its blocks guard hazards that exist only in the source repo. Dropping those is correct — porting them is cargo — but dropping them SILENTLY leaves two files that present as the same guard and are not, with no stated reason for the difference. The next reader has two bad options and no way to choose between them: re-add the block as cargo (now guarding nothing, and the guard costs friction for no protection), or conclude the source repo's copy is bloated and delete it there (removing a guard that is load-bearing where it lives). Both are worse than the divergence itself. The fix is cheap and belongs in the code, not the commit message: leave the section header, say which hazard it guards, say why that hazard cannot occur here, and name the concrete trigger that should cause it to be re-added. Generalizes to any fleet sharing harness code across repos — the divergence is inevitable and fine; the undocumented divergence is the bug.
entry.title: A ported guard must document the blocks it deliberately did not port

raw: [L0001] A ported guard must document the blocks it deliberately did not port | candidate | added: 2026-08-12 | tags: foundations-seams | lesson: When harness code (a hook, a gate, a lint) is copied between sibling repos, some of its blocks guard hazards that exist only in the source repo. Dropping those is correct — porting them is cargo — but dropping them SILENTLY leaves two files that present as the same guard and are not, with no stated reason for the difference. The next reader has two bad options and no way to choose between them: re-add the block as cargo (now guarding nothing, and the guard costs friction for no protection), or conclude the source repo's copy is bloated and delete it there (removing a guard that is load-bearing where it lives). Both are worse than the divergence itself. The fix is cheap and belongs in the code, not the commit message: leave the section header, say which hazard it guards, say why that hazard cannot occur here, and name the concrete trigger that should cause it to be re-added. Generalizes to any fleet sharing harness code across repos — the divergence is inevitable and fine; the undocumented divergence is the bug. | evidence: plainsynth's `.claude/hooks/pretool-deny.sh` was ported from FOUNDATIONS' copy at spin-up (2026-08-12) to inherit its hard-won fixes — per-segment argument parsing, heredoc stripping, force-push flag placement, each of which had cost a real false positive or a real hole there. One block did not apply: FOUNDATIONS refuses broad stages (`git add -A`) because a CONSUMER may file into its `integrations/<name>/` mailbox mid-command, a race PreToolUse structurally cannot see. plainsynth is a pure consumer with no inbound mailbox, so the hazard cannot occur. It was dropped and replaced in-place with a `# --- NOT PORTED:` block stating the hazard, why it is impossible here, and the re-add trigger ("the moment this repo acquires an `integrations/<someone>/` directory another project's residents may write to"). Recorded in DECISIONS #3. | falsifier: The failure mode here is PREDICTED, not yet observed — no session has yet mis-handled a silent divergence in this fleet. This entry is wrong if a shared guard diverges silently between two repos and a later session reconciles it correctly anyway (from git history, from the DECISIONS log, or by re-deriving the hazard), showing the in-code note was ceremony. It is also wrong if the notes themselves rot — if a `NOT PORTED` block's re-add trigger is observed to go stale and mislead a session more than the bare absence would have, the practice is a net negative and should be replaced by "diverge freely, reconcile from the source repo on demand".

entry.evidence: 2026-08-12, FOUNDATIONS' `note_shadow` (the forensic dump replay tool). plainsynth's intake brief asked them to confirm the dump format rather than infer it from their HYPERSAW sample, per SPEC.md's instruction not to invent formats. Answering made them test the parser against a non-HYPERSAW producer for the first time: it keyed voice rows on the literal string `core0[`, a HYPERSAW spelling. They planted a textbook orphan in a dump naming its rows `voice0[` and got `ok D1/D2: ... (0 voice row(s) checked)` / `note_shadow: GREEN` — a vacuous pass in the tool built to catch precisely that class of defect. Their fifth recorded instance of a check that cannot fire, and the first found by a QUESTION rather than a run: no plainsynth byte had been emitted. Fixed by keying on the required `-- key` tag and adding an S3 check that makes unreadable voice-section lines RED; both pinned as regression fixtures. Recorded here as DECISIONS #10; theirs as #65.
entry.falsifier: A verifier whose empty-selection case is genuinely correct to report as pass — i.e. where "nothing to examine" is a real and expected state that carries no information loss (an incremental linter over a changed-files list that is legitimately empty is the likely counter-case). If that class is common, the rule is too broad and should narrow to "assert the count wherever the selector encodes an assumption about input shape". This entry is also wrong if the count assertion proves to generate more false alarms than the vacuous passes it catches.
entry.lesson: Any verifier that (a) selects a set of things to examine and (b) reports pass/fail over that set has a silent failure mode: if selection returns EMPTY, the assertion is vacuously true and the tool prints GREEN. The output of "nothing was wrong" and "nothing was looked at" is the same string, so the defect is invisible in exactly the artifact you would use to find it — and it is worst in the tools built to catch other tools' blind spots, because those are trusted most and re-checked least. The selection step is usually where producer-specific assumptions hide: a literal name, a spelling, a path shape that was true of the one input the tool was developed against. Two fixes, and you need both: make the selector key on something SEMANTIC (a tag the format requires) rather than on incidental naming; and make unparseable-but-present input RED rather than absent, because "no items" and "no items I understood" must not collapse into one report. Assert the count, never just the predicate. Generalizes far past parsers — linters with a file glob, test collectors, migration scripts, any grep-based gate. Corollary for consumers: never accept a green from someone else's tool without reading how many things it says it examined.

entry.evidence: descending walk `G F E D C` → C Natural Minor — conform returns `G F F D C` (4 distinct of 5; destroyed even at EQUAL cardinality), remap returns `G F D♯ D C` (5 distinct, intact); remap to Minor Pentatonic raises ValueError. Provider notice notice-conform-vs-remap.md; adopt-conform-vs-remap.md.
entry.falsifier: the engine gains a walk-aware conform, or span-policy knobs land (their gap 31(b)/(c)) making unequal-cardinality translation possible — either would change the routing advice, not the conform/remap distinction itself.
entry.lesson: Two engine tools both take "a scale and a root" and return notes, and choosing wrong silently gives the user something else. `conform_to_scale` answers "make these notes LEGAL in S" — proximity, many-to-one, lossy, for cleanup. `remap_by_degree` answers "TRANSLATE this into S" — degree→degree, bijective on in-scale material, walks survive by construction. A user who picks a scale from a dropdown to "make it Dorian" means **translate**; routing that into conform destroys scale walks (and Ableton's own Scale tool has the same failure, for the same reason). `fit_to_key` is merely a preset of conform. **The two are distinguished by user intent, which the signatures do not reveal** — so the UI must name the difference, including which one merges notes. Unequal cardinality (7 degrees → 5) makes translation impossible by pigeonhole; the engine refuses with a legible reason, and surfacing that refusal is correct behaviour, not an error to hide.
entry.supersedes_note: (but CORRECTS a same-day conclusion in this repo that fit/conform equivalence implied one UI control; the equivalence is real, the inference was not)

entry.evidence: 20-note clip sent with block chords first, melody second — input onsets `0,0,0,2,2,2,4,4,4,6,6,6,0,1,...` returned as `0,0,0,0,1,2,2,2,2,3,...`. Positional comparison claimed 17 notes moved where the engine reported 10; edit-based pairing reproduces the engine's counts exactly (2/8/10/3) with zero unmatched edits. Filed upstream as brief tonality-live-002.
entry.falsifier: the provider takes option (1) of that brief and assembles output by original index — then input order IS preserved and positional pairing becomes valid (but pairing via `edits` still works, so prefer it regardless).
entry.lesson: `conform_to_scale` / `fit_to_key` return `events` **sorted by onset**, not in the order they were sent, even though the docstring says "in the input's note order". So `output[i]` is not `input[i]`. Writing the result to `clip.notes` is unaffected (note order is meaningless in a MIDI clip) and collision dedupe is safe (it keys on pitch+onset+duration), but ANY before/after pairing must go through `report.edits`, matching `(onset, from_midi)` → `to_midi`. A positional diff is silently wrong, not loudly wrong.

entry.evidence: life-os-app VPS, verified live 2026-08-14 in response to autonomous-lifeos-001: `bootstrap.sh`'s sed had run, `sshd -T` showed `passwordauthentication yes`; tens of thousands of failed-password attempts in 30d had been hitting an endpoint the script believed was closed (bounded by a locked deploy-account password + `PermitRootLogin no`, so no breach — a defense-in-depth gap). Fixed with the 00- drop-in + `sshd -T` assertion in `bootstrap.sh`; password auth verified refused from outside. Filed by the Life-OS resident via autonomous-lifeos-001 response-1; Promoted from life-os-app#L0002 (their copy: tier candidate, tags deploy-ops/security).
entry.falsifier: on a stock Ubuntu cloud image with a conflicting `50-cloud-init.conf`, `sshd -T` shows the sed'd main-file value taking effect.
entry.lesson: Ubuntu's stock `sshd_config` `Include`s `sshd_config.d/*.conf` near the TOP, and OpenSSH takes the FIRST value it meets for each keyword. So a hardening script that `sed`s `PasswordAuthentication no` into the main file is silently overridden by cloud-init's `50-cloud-init.conf` (`PasswordAuthentication yes`), and the file LOOKS hardened while the effective config is not. Write your own `00-<project>-hardening.conf` (sorts first, so it wins over anything cloud-init writes later) and ASSERT the effective config with `sshd -T`, never by reading the file — prove the result, not the artifact. Generalizes to every cloud-image box the fleet deploys.

entry.evidence: leak_scan.py 2026-07-13 (dead absolute-path detection, caught only by testing against a known-bad); life-os-app `verify` ip_gate 2026-08-14 (planted the real leaked IP, 0 hits, root cause `\b`). Antiphon L0001 records the same rule from the consumer side.
entry.falsifier: a `git grep -E` invocation where `\s`/`\d`/`\b` demonstrably matches — would mean git grep gained PCRE by default and this rule can retire (check `git grep -P` availability first; that is a different flag).
entry.lesson: `git grep -E` does not support Perl-class escapes. A pattern using `\s`, `\d` or `\b` does not error; it matches NOTHING, and the gate ships permanently green. Three independent instances in five weeks: `\s` in the first leak_scan (all findings were coming from the username pattern alone), then `\b` in life-os-app's ip_gate (would never have flagged the very IP it was written for). The only defense that catches this class is procedural: before trusting any new detector, plant a KNOWN-BAD line and watch it fire, plant a KNOWN-GOOD near-miss and watch it stay quiet, then run the clean tree. Comment the trap at the pattern site — the next agent will "simplify" it back.

entry.evidence: (fleet-origin, first proof-site life-os-app) CI first run 2026-08-14 (`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'` on the runner; local venv on 1.28.1 fine); migration verified 8/8 tools registering on 2.0.0 fresh + 246 tests green on both.
entry.falsifier: an MCP-server repo in the fleet with `mcp>=1.0` that installs clean on 2.x without the fallback — would mean it never used the moved path, and this is a per-import-path issue, not a fleet-wide one.
entry.lesson: `mcp>=1.0` in requirements resolves to 2.0.0 on a fresh install; the 1.x `FastMCP` import path is gone and the server fails at import. Local venvs created before the release keep working, so the break is invisible until CI or a new machine — exactly the "works on my venv" shape. Working migration (life-os-app): try `from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer as FastMCP` first, fall back to `from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP` — same `.tool()`/`.run()` API, so one file runs on both. Prove it BOTH ways (fresh 2.0 venv AND the old pinned one) before dropping any pin. THE SHIM IS SAFE ONLY ON THE SHARED API SURFACE — `.tool()` decorator and `.run()` with stdio default. A server that reached into 1.x-specific FastMCP internals is NOT rescued by the fallback and needs a real migration. So the retrofit check for each of the ten remaining MCP-server repos is "does the server touch anything beyond `@tool`/`.run()`?", not "does the import resolve" — the second passes on a shim that will fail at first call.

entry.evidence: ball_scan.py 2026-08-09, found by answering "is there a HYPERSAW brief?" against FOUNDATIONS' mailbox; fixed with `_ball_token` + tests seeded from the OTHER repos' forms. dispatch-001's four-named-findings fixture is the positive case: it pinned granularity the provider would not have thought to.
entry.falsifier: a provider-authored fixture set that surfaces a consumer's dialect without any consumer input — possible only if the provider deliberately samples every consumer's corpus, which is the consumer-authorship rule by another name.
entry.lesson: A detector or parser tested only against fixtures drawn from its own repo's files is tested only against the conventions that repo already follows. `ball_scan` matched the `ball:` field by whole string because autonomous writes bare tokens; FOUNDATIONS and Tonality write `ball: provider (please review…)`, so every annotated obligation ON autonomous read as not-ours — a false negative in the check whose job was not losing work — and no fixture buildable from autonomous's own mailbox would ever have shown it. INTEGRATIONS already says contract tests are consumer-authored; this is the mechanism-level reason WHY that rule is load-bearing, not etiquette.

entry.evidence: FOUNDATIONS' CI carried the kit template's `paths-ignore: ["**/*.md","docs/**"]` while its oracle is almost entirely markdown/JSON consistency (INDEX↔LIBRARY, manifest survey answers, correspondent registry, contract version). Every green tick on a docs change had run nothing. Removing the filter (PR #1, 2026-08-10) turned CI red in 6s and exposed two gates broken the whole time: the correspondent sweep failed off the dev machine because it treated absent sibling repos as our data being wrong (a machine detector, not a check), and the standby-notice hash was computed, printed, and compared to no baseline while its own comment claimed it detected un-versioned edits. Both verified fixed against a HOME-redirected CI simulation before pushing (DECISIONS #28).
entry.falsifier: A project where path-filtered CI ran zero times on a whole class of change over many months and no defect reached the branch — or a case where observing a gate fail on purpose cost more than the defects it would have caught. Also falsified if the simulated-environment discipline turns out to produce false confidence, i.e. a simulation that passes where the real runner fails.
entry.lesson: Two failure modes hide behind the same green tick and both survive indefinitely because the signal for "ran and passed" is identical to the signal for "did not run" and to "ran a check that cannot fail". (a) A CI path filter that skips the job entirely — the badge is green, the coverage is zero, and nobody looks because nothing is red. (b) A check whose result is computed and then never compared to anything, which passes on every input including wrong ones. The countermeasure is not more checks but observing each gate FAIL once on purpose, and — for environment-sensitive checks — running the suite in a simulated foreign environment locally rather than discovering machine dependence through a push/wait/read cycle in public.
entry.recurred: 2026-08-10 — and the recurrence sharpened the lesson. A THIRD mode sits beside the two above and is worse than either: CI that runs, FAILS LOUDLY, and is never read. FOUNDATIONS' main was red for nine consecutive runs across two days (2026-08-08 21:03 → 2026-08-10) while the local oracle was green, and the agent asserted "CI passing" in a delivered artifact on the strength of one check made before the breakage. Not indistinguishable-from-passing — simply unobserved. The distinction matters for the countermeasure: filters and dead checks are fixed by testing gates, but an unread signal is fixed only by something that READS it. Concrete mitigation: `./verify ci` queries main's published conclusion (kept out of `fast`, which must stay offline), charter-bound to run at phase gates. entry.evidence: Three occurrences in one week in FOUNDATIONS. (1) An orphan-reply check reported 9 hits; 8 were its own resolver — `in-reply-to` names a document *id* in most threads and a *filename* in others, and v1 resolved only filenames (DECISIONS #66). (2) An examined-count added to the correspondent sweep printed "0 repo(s) scanned" while still passing — the counter was wired to a source line absent from that function; the true number was 60 (#67). (3) A README-vs-filesystem check flagged `modules/` as a lie where the README honestly said "empty — `_template/` is the intake form" (#68). All three would have shipped as noise.
entry.falsifier: A sustained period where new checks' first runs are predominantly true positives — i.e. authors' state models are reliable enough that "suspect the check first" costs more than it saves.
entry.lesson: When a newly written check fires against state you believe is good, the base rate strongly favours the check being wrong, not the state. Explain EVERY hit before trusting it — including the ones you like. The danger is asymmetric: a check that under-fires is invisible, but a check that over-fires reads as noise and gets switched off within days, taking its true positives with it. Counterpart to L0005: that rule gets the check BUILT, this one gets it BELIEVED.

entry.evidence: FOUNDATIONS' pre-commit guard blocked broad `git add -A` staging only while a consumer's filing sat pending in the mailbox. A consumer filed mid-Bash-call — after the hook's check ran, before the `add` executed — and the filing was swept into an unrelated commit. Fourth occurrence of the violation the guard existed to prevent, and the second committed by the tooling built to stop it. Fixed by blocking broad stages unconditionally: a command that names its files cannot sweep a filing it never saw (DECISIONS #55).
entry.falsifier: A sampling guard that provably closes its window without removing the operation — an atomic check-and-act at the same layer as the mutation. Where such a primitive exists, this does not apply.
entry.lesson: Any guard that checks a condition then permits an action has a window between the two, and anything that can change the condition inside that window defeats it — permanently, not intermittently. Widening the check does not close it; only removing the window does. Make the safe path the ONLY path (refuse the broad operation outright, so there is nothing to sample) rather than sampling better. Recognisable whenever a guard's correctness argument contains "we check first" — that phrasing IS the window. The shape is TOCTOU, but it recurs in process tooling where people do not expect it.

entry.evidence: Two independent arrivals. (1) FOUNDATIONS' §3.3 preset-cascade paper specified storing values relative to a scope's defaults, a literal reading of its own constitution; the prototype's FIRST property run failed the constitution's identity invariant on seed 0 at the 11th digit. Amended to store absolutely with a basis snapshot, deriving the delta only on a genuine rebase (DECISIONS #62). (2) HYPERSAW reached the same rule independently for its inertia knob, which stores its own domain because "squaring the core value back is not bit-exact, and state_check demands exact round-trips".
entry.falsifier: A round-trip provably surviving arithmetic for all representable inputs — integer or fixed-point domains, or a float scheme where the transformation is exactly invertible.
entry.lesson: If a system promises that save-then-load returns the ORIGINAL value, the round-trip path must not compute. Store what you must return verbatim and derive the transformed form only when a transformation is genuinely requested. In IEEE 754 `(v - b) + b != v` for ordinary values, so any "store the delta, add the base on load" scheme silently violates a bit-exactness invariant a specification may state one paragraph earlier. General rule: when an invariant and a storage convention conflict, the INVARIANT outranks the convention — the convention was a means to it.

entry.evidence: FOUNDATIONS read a consumer's intake brief staged in the consumer's own tree, marked `status: draft — awaiting human carriage`, `filed: (not yet)`, `ball: provider, once filed`. It was answered, the consumer registered, and the change merged — collapsing the filing step the author had deliberately left open and costing them the revision pass filing exists for. Caught by the author, not by us (DECISIONS #66). Now checked mechanically: a reply whose `in-reply-to` names a document this tree does not hold is reported.
entry.falsifier: A corpus where status fields are stale often enough that trusting them causes more errors than ignoring them — there the field is noise and the body is the better signal.
entry.lesson: A workflow that reads documents without reading what they say ABOUT THEMSELVES will execute drafts. Presence on disk is not readiness; `status:`, `draft`, `filed`, `ball:` exist precisely because the body alone cannot say whether it is ready to be acted on. This survives a "derive, don't recall" discipline — you can derive faithfully from the wrong half of the document. Agent workflows are unusually exposed: a human skimming notices "DRAFT" at the top; a process that greps for content does not.

entry.evidence: Two independent instances. (1) HYPERSAW used "voice" for four different things — a note identity (`VoiceTag`), the allocation unit (`Swarm`, never called a voice), note-level policy ("Voice: Mono"), and a member within a voice ("Per-Voice Env"). Three turns of a live field investigation hunted a "stuck voice" that never existed while the human was describing a late NOTE-off; it turned over in one reading once the terms were separated (DECISIONS #59, origin HYPERSAW). (2) FOUNDATIONS shipped `VoiceTable`/`VoiceHandle` for what the field calls notes, caught by a prior-art probe hours after the code existed and renamed at zero consumers (#53/#54).
entry.falsifier: A domain where a deliberately overloaded term demonstrably aids communication and no investigation has been misdirected by it — context resolves the ambiguity reliably in practice.
entry.lesson: Ambiguous vocabulary does not merely confuse readers — it corrupts investigation, because evidence refuting a hypothesis under meaning A gets filed under meaning B and never lands. The wrong noun keeps a wrong MODEL alive. Vocabulary is therefore a correctness concern, not a style one, and it argues for renaming BEFORE an interface hardens: a mechanical rename early versus a breaking change plus a live misdiagnosis later. Adopt the field's existing word rather than minting one.

entry.evidence: FOUNDATIONS commissioned a test instrument (plainsynth) to exercise its own seams. The correspondent registry counted `direction: consumes`, and that count is what the two-consumer rule leans on; registering the testbed as a consumer would have moved it 8 → 9, overstating independent evidence with a project the provider built itself. Filed instead under a third role, `direction: validates`, with the sweep reporting "8 consumers + 3 providers + 1 validator (not consumers)" (DECISIONS #65). The general shape was named by plainsynth — their own warning about self-confirmation, applied one level up to the bookkeeping.
entry.falsifier: A roster where a mixed-kind member provably distorts no decision the count feeds — every consumer of the count already re-filters by kind, making the aggregate decorative.
entry.lesson: When a COUNT is used as evidence for a rule ("two independent consumers before we generalise", "three sources before we publish"), the register producing that count acquires a correctness requirement its schema usually does not state: every member must be the KIND of thing the rule means. Admitting a different kind does not merely mislabel a row — it makes the NUMBER lie, and the number is what the rule consumes. Fix with a distinct role in the schema plus a counter that reports kinds separately, never a comment.

raw: [L0012] A boundary breach that arrives as a GIFT is the hardest kind to refuse | candidate | added: 2026-08-12 | tags: contract-generality, extraction-discipline | lesson: The boundary rules a project writes down are tested hardest not by someone pushing against them but by someone OFFERING to cross them helpfully — a provider handing a validator a criterion to close, a senior party inviting a junior one past a limit that exists to protect the work. The asymmetry is social, not technical: refusing feels ungracious and accepting feels collaborative, and NEITHER FEELING IS EVIDENCE. Two practical consequences. (1) The party being offered the crossing is usually the only one positioned to refuse it, because the offering party experiences the offer as generosity and will not audit it. (2) A rule of the form "no promotion may be argued from X's evidence alone" needs an explicit companion — "and X should refuse an invitation to supply it" — or the rule can be routed around from the protected side, with permission, which is the only way it could ever happen. | evidence: FOUNDATIONS built invariant harnesses for F2 acceptance criterion 1b, then told plainsynth — a testbed FOUNDATIONS itself commissioned, registered under a distinct `validates` role carrying "zero generality weight" precisely so its evidence would not be counted — that the criterion "closes when a CONSUMER runs these against real DSP … which is a thing you can do and we cannot". plainsynth refused, on two grounds the provider had missed: their DSP is deliberately boring BY THE PROVIDER'S OWN COMMISSION, so a repo boundary is not an independence boundary; and the criterion's own closing sentence said it exists so the extraction phase cannot certify a shared defect into the frozen contract — which only re-pointed code can discharge. The provider's ROADMAP edit had contradicted that sentence three lines above it. Ruled in the refuser's favour, DECISIONS

entry.evidence: One consumer found three in the same library. `kLeafShadowsAncestor`'s comment was narrower than the check in both directions; `kParam`'s said "a registry parameter", inventing a constraint the code never had and stopping half a phase (the header did not even include the registry); `scope_selector`'s said `"" = global` while the same header declared the field uninterpreted with semantics deferred — and the project's own shipped cascade already treated empty as unrestricted (DECISIONS #90, #93). In all three the code was correct.
entry.falsifier: A codebase whose consumers demonstrably read the implementation before the comment — in which case comment drift costs nothing and the effort belongs elsewhere.
entry.lesson: A consumer builds against what the header SAYS, not against what the code does. So a comment that merely misdescribes is not a documentation defect to fix later — it is a wrong interface, shipping now, and it will be obeyed. The severe case is a declaration-only artefact (a doorframe, a schema, an unimplemented field): it declares a shape and evaluates nothing, so its comments ARE most of its interface, and a comment asserting semantics the same file says do not exist yet is self-contradictory in a way no test can catch.

entry.evidence: A routing doorframe documented `scope_selector = ""` as "global". A consumer with eight voices had one address naming eight envelope outputs; their per-voice routings validated while asserting they were global. They filed it rather than work around it, and the same defect was found in the neighbouring `distribution` field — introduced by a comment that explicitly mirrored the one being fixed (DECISIONS #93).
entry.falsifier: A field whose default genuinely is the overwhelmingly common case AND whose consumers can express the alternative from day one — then a meaningful default costs nothing and an absence adds ceremony.
entry.lesson: An unimplemented field needs a trivial value, and the temptation is to give it the "obvious" default — empty means global, zero means uniform, null means all. That makes every consumer who cannot yet express the truth write something FALSE that validates, and nothing anywhere distinguishes "I mean the default" from "I could not say". The falsehood is silent, uniform across consumers, and accumulating: the first implementation inherits a corpus of untrue declarations that all passed. Define the placeholder as an absence — "not expressed" — which is true for everyone, and require the eventual semantics to SPELL its own default rather than inherit the placeholder.

entry.evidence: A note-lifecycle suite failed a consumer twice on cases that pinned WHEN the library retires an identity, while the ruling only said an identity may leave through a path that delivers its END — which the consumer satisfied, measured, 38 issued and 38 delivered. A third case asserted a within-class steal order the library's own header assigned to the engine as private policy (DECISIONS #85). All three shipped as rulings.
entry.falsifier: A domain where the provider's implementation IS the specification by fiat — a reference implementation whose behaviour is normative — in which case encoding and ruling are the same thing.
entry.lesson: When a provider turns rulings into a conformance suite, the cases quietly encode HOW the provider's own implementation satisfies each rule alongside WHAT was ruled. A consumer that honours every rule by different means then fails, and is told it is broken when it is conforming. Classify every case explicitly: a RULING (all consumers must satisfy) or the provider's ENCODING (reported as divergence, never as failure). Keep the classification in the provider's artefact, never in the consumer's adapter — a consumer that can declare its way out of a ruled case has an opt-out, not a category.

entry.evidence: A registry claimed a contract "active — shipped" while the header did not exist at the consumer's pin; the consumer found it and declined to file it as a defect because they could not tell whose error it was (DECISIONS #78). Later the same provider shipped a conformance suite, filed two notices about it, and told nobody which commit to pin — while a consumer whose roadmap said it was waiting stayed blocked (DECISIONS #92).
entry.falsifier: An ecosystem where consumers track a moving branch rather than pinning, so "obtainable" has no meaning and freshness is the only property.
entry.lesson: A provider announcing a facility describes its own HEAD; a consumer can only have what its pin can reach. Recording the commit where a thing first appeared is not enough — if it was corrected afterwards, a consumer pinning the first commit adopts the version you have since found defects in, with your announcement as the warrant. Record the commit where the artefact is correct, and re-record it when it is corrected. The second-order failure is quieter: publishing a facility does not tell a consumer WHICH commit to pin, so a consumer can sit blocked on a file that exists and that they cannot see.

entry.evidence: Three occurrences in one week in one suite. A leak pin asserted an end state the bug did not change (SURVIVED under mutation). A short-circuit pin was anchored to an assertion that was later removed as unsatisfiable, so it silently stopped planting anything. Its re-anchor also failed, because the drive it was moved to ran in an earlier case that discarded the result (DECISIONS #84, #87, #88).
entry.falsifier: A suite where every assertion is generated from the specification rather than written after a fix, so no assertion has a fix-shaped anchor to drift from.
entry.lesson: A pin written after a fix is anchored to whatever the fixed code happens to do, which is not the same as being sensitive to the bug. Reintroduce the defect and require the pin to go red. Two ways it silently fails: the pin asserts something the bug does not disturb, or a later change removes the very construct the pin was anchored to, leaving it green and measuring nothing. The second is worse because it happens long after anyone is looking.

entry.evidence: 2026-08-12, FOUNDATIONS' `note_shadow` (the forensic dump replay tool). plainsynth's intake brief asked them to confirm the dump format rather than infer it from their HYPERSAW sample, per SPEC.md's instruction not to invent formats. Answering made them test the parser against a non-HYPERSAW producer for the first time: it keyed voice rows on the literal string `core0[`, a HYPERSAW spelling. They planted a textbook orphan in a dump naming its rows `voice0[` and got `ok D1/D2: ... (0 voice row(s) checked)` / `note_shadow: GREEN` — a vacuous pass in the tool built to catch precisely that class of defect. Their fifth recorded instance of a check that cannot fire, and the first found by a QUESTION rather than a run: no plainsynth byte had been emitted. Fixed by keying on the required `-- key` tag and adding an S3 check that makes unreadable voice-section lines RED; both pinned as regression fixtures. Recorded here as DECISIONS #10; theirs as #65. | recurrence (basis for canonical, and the independence is qualified deliberately): THREE further instances the same day, in two codebases. (a) FOUNDATIONS' correspondent sweep — five green lines phrased as absences, none stating a denominator; all five now report counts and two REFUSE zero (their DECISIONS #67). (b) Their instrumentation of (a) was itself caught by the rule within ten minutes: `discovery: 0 repo(s) scanned` printed `ok`. (c) plainsynth's own `./verify` had the same defect while we were telling them about theirs — `leak_gate` passed on an empty `git grep` (identical output whether the tree is clean or the search scanned nothing) and the INDEX<->LIBRARY check compared two regex-derived sets that an entry-format change empties together. Both instrumented and both zero-refusals calibrated with planted defects (NC9: an over-broad `.leakcheck-allow` entry silently disabling the whole gate — a real hazard, previously reported as a confident `ok`; NC10: an entry-format change emptying both sides). QUALIFICATION for the parent audit loop: (a) and (b) are independent in OCCURRENCE but not in DISCOVERY — they were found by applying this rule, not by arriving at it separately. (c) is the strongest datum, because it was found by turning the rule on the project that wrote it, which is the direction a lesson is least likely to be pointed. | relation (added 2026-08-12, correcting this entry's implied novelty): FOUNDATIONS already held `[L0005]` — *"a gate never observed to fail has not been tested; skipped CI is indistinguishable from passing"*, canonical, added 2026-08-10 — whose clause (b) is "a check whose result is computed and then never compared to anything". That is the PARENT family, and it predates this entry by two days. Their `registry.h` AT OUR PIN cites it in-code while removing an unreachable `kAmbiguousCoreKey` check, so the family was live on their side before our brief was written. Discovered here on 2026-08-12 while reading the pinned headers for ROADMAP P1 — i.e. after this entry was promoted, not before. What is genuinely ours is narrower than the title suggests: not "checks can be vacuous" (theirs) but the DENOMINATOR mechanism — an assertion phrased as an absence has no denominator; state what was examined; make zero refuse. Their countermeasure was behavioural (observe each gate fail once on purpose); ours is structural (the count is in the output and the zero is rejected), and the two compose rather than compete. FLAG FOR THE PARENT AUDIT LOOP: do not promote this upward as an independent discovery. If it meets a sibling holding L0005 or its equivalent, MERGE into that entry as a mechanism, do not add a second one — two entries for one family is how a library starts arguing with itself. Tier stays canonical: the recurrence that earned it (this project's own oracle, found by turning the rule inward) is real regardless of who named the family first.
entry.falsifier: A verifier whose empty-selection case is genuinely correct to report as pass — i.e. where "nothing to examine" is a real and expected state that carries no information loss (an incremental linter over a changed-files list that is legitimately empty is the likely counter-case). If that class is common, the rule is too broad and should narrow to "assert the count wherever the selector encodes an assumption about input shape". This entry is also wrong if the count assertion proves to generate more false alarms than the vacuous passes it catches.
entry.lesson: Any verifier that (a) selects a set of things to examine and (b) reports pass/fail over that set has a silent failure mode: if selection returns EMPTY, the assertion is vacuously true and the tool prints GREEN. The output of "nothing was wrong" and "nothing was looked at" is the same string, so the defect is invisible in exactly the artifact you would use to find it — and it is worst in the tools built to catch other tools' blind spots, because those are trusted most and re-checked least. The selection step is usually where producer-specific assumptions hide: a literal name, a spelling, a path shape that was true of the one input the tool was developed against. Two fixes, and you need both: make the selector key on something SEMANTIC (a tag the format requires) rather than on incidental naming; and make unparseable-but-present input RED rather than absent, because "no items" and "no items I understood" must not collapse into one report. Assert the count, never just the predicate. Generalizes far past parsers — linters with a file glob, test collectors, migration scripts, any grep-based gate. Corollary for consumers: never accept a green from someone else's tool without reading how many things it says it examined. | extension (2026-08-12, the promotion): the fix must be OUTPUT, not principle, and the count must not be DECORATIVE. Two distinct failures were observed the same day the rule was written. (i) Agreeing with the rule surfaces nothing: FOUNDATIONS adopted it and found five absence-phrased `ok` lines only by instrumenting them to print denominators — reasoning about which checks "might" be vacuous had found none. (ii) A printed count nobody checks is decoration: their first instrumented run printed `discovery: 0 repo(s) scanned` and STILL said `ok`, because nothing refused the zero. The counter had been wired to a line that did not exist; the true number was 60. So wherever zero is impossible-if-working, zero must REFUSE to pass, not merely be visible. The tell that you have the weak version is that your green lines are phrased as absences ("no leaks", "no orphans", "nothing awaiting") — an absence has no denominator, and that is the whole defect in one grammatical habit.

entry.evidence: plainsynth's `provider_gate` in `./verify`, 2026-08-12. It asserts the pinned FOUNDATIONS commit is reachable in the sibling checkout, explicitly NOT that their HEAD equals our pin. Within the hours of a single session their HEAD moved FOUR times (`6b4fa90` -> `9e4b4a2` -> `d25396d` -> `6d47bd8`) while our pin correctly stayed at `6b4fa90`; the gate stayed green and printed the divergence as an informational note each time. The fourth move landed while this very entry was being written, which is the cleanest demonstration available that the cadence of a sibling repo is not a signal about us. An equality gate would have gone red four times in one day, never once for a reason concerning us or actionable by us. Recorded as DECISIONS #5. CREDIT, so the parent audit loop does not double-count this as independent convergence: the underlying principle — "an alert that can never clear is noise that trains you to stop reading the tool" — was READ this session in FOUNDATIONS' `integrations/correspondents.json` (`_deferred_note`), not independently derived here. What is new is the construction (obtainability-not-equality) and the same-day observation of the counterfactual.
entry.falsifier: A dependency where tracking HEAD genuinely IS the requirement (an unpinned rolling integration, a monorepo sibling built from source every time) — there, equality is the property and this lesson does not apply. More seriously, this is wrong if obtainability turns out to be too weak a proxy: if builds against a pin start failing while the pin remains reachable (a moved tag, a force-pushed branch leaving the commit reachable but the tree different), the gate is checking reachability where it should check CONTENT, and the fix is a tree hash rather than a `cat-file -e`. Watch for the first "verify was green and the build was broken" — that is this entry failing.
entry.lesson: When a check asserts something about an EXTERNAL system you do not control, the naive construction compares that system's CURRENT state to your recorded expectation — and it is almost always wrong. The dependency moves for reasons that have nothing to do with you, so the gate fires constantly, correctly, and uselessly; and a gate that is red for reasons the reader cannot act on is one people learn to skip, which costs you the real failure later. Ask instead: what property do I actually depend on? Usually it is not "their state equals my record" but "the thing I pinned is still OBTAINABLE" — stable by construction, and false only when something is genuinely wrong (history rewritten, remote pruned, checkout stale). Then report the divergence as INFORMATION beside the pass: you do want to know they moved, you just do not want that to be a failure. The general form: a gate's red condition must be something the person reading it can act on. If the only available action is "acknowledge the world changed", it is a log line, not a gate.

entry.evidence: 2026-08-12, plainsynth's intake into FOUNDATIONS. Our brief warned them not to count our evidence toward their two-consumer rule, because a library validated against its own testbed is the library agreeing with itself. Their resident applied that warning ONE LEVEL UP, to their own bookkeeping: filing plainsynth under `direction: consumes` would have moved their correspondent roster from 8 to 9, and that count is the number the two-consumer rule leans on — so the roster itself would have begun overstating how much independent evidence existed, with every individual entry correct. They created a third role (`direction: validates`) rather than an annotated consumer, and their sweep now reports "8 consumers + 3 providers + 1 validator (not consumers)". CREDIT, and this entry exists because of a correction: our ack called this "a better catch than the one we filed", and their reply (DECISIONS #67) corrected us — it was our warning, applied one level up, and the sentence shape is ours to keep. Miscrediting it is why it was not already written down here.
entry.falsifier: A roster where an annotated member is genuinely safe — where every consumer of the count reads the annotation, reliably, over time. If that holds in practice, the cheaper fix (a flag on the row) beats inventing a kind, and this entry is over-engineering. It is also wrong if proliferating kinds turns out to cost more than the miscount: a registry that grows a new role for every edge case becomes unqueryable, and at that point the right move is one `counts_toward` boolean rather than N roles. Watch for the third role added in a month — that is this entry failing.
entry.lesson: When a policy leans on the SIZE of a set — "we generalize once two independent consumers need it", "promote after three sightings", "quorum is a majority of reviewers" — the set silently acquires a second job it was never designed for. It started as a directory of who exists; it is now an evidence counter. The failure is that admitting a member who does not carry the property being counted is locally correct and globally wrong: nobody lies, the roster is accurate, and the number it produces is inflated. Nobody notices, because the count is read as a count and never as a claim. Two defences. (1) When a new member does not carry the counted property, give it a DIFFERENT KIND rather than an asterisk — a separate role, direction, or list — because a footnote lives in the roster and the count is computed from the rows. (2) Make the summary state the composition, not just the total ("8 consumers + 3 providers + 1 validator"), so the denominator's makeup is visible at the point of use. Note the shape shared with L0002: both are about a number that is read without its basis. Generalizes to review quorums, test-suite counts that gate a release, dataset class balance, SLA sample sizes — anywhere cardinality has been quietly promoted from description to argument.
entry.title: A roster whose cardinality is load-bearing must not admit a member of a different kind

entry.evidence: 2026-08-12, FOUNDATIONS' `brief-invariant-harness.md`. They offered plainsynth their invariant harness and wrote that their F2 acceptance criterion 1b "needs an invariant oracle run against real DSP", that "toy engines in our own test do not count", and that it "closes when a consumer runs these — which is a thing you can do and we cannot, and is precisely the division your validator role was created for". Two things made that unsafe to accept, and both were checkable rather than matters of taste: (a) plainsynth's DSP is a toy BY THEIR OWN COMMISSION — SPEC.md, written by their resident, specifies "a deliberately boring generic synth (sine, saw, noise; the DSP is not the subject)" and our charter forbids DSP novelty — so a sine oscillator here is not more real than one in their test, and the difference is a repo boundary rather than an independence boundary; (b) their own DECISIONS #65 created the validator role expressly so we would NOT be counted as a consumer, and 1b as stated closes on a consumer run. Declined in `response-invariant-harness.md` §3, with the ruling handed back to them and the alternative contribution named (calibrating their harness, which a toy engine is a perfectly good vehicle for). Recorded as plainsynth DECISIONS #18. The offer was caught on first reading; the failure did not occur, and this entry exists so the next one is caught too. | falsifier-tested (2026-08-12, and it survived): the falsifier below named FOUNDATIONS' pending ruling as the disconfirming outcome. They ruled the OTHER way (their DECISIONS #74): a plainsynth run is not weak evidence for criterion 1b, it is ORTHOGONAL to it — the criterion exists so extraction cannot certify a defect shared by the library and HYPERSAW, which only RE-POINTED code can discharge. So the discount was about independence after all, and refusing was correct. A falsifier that was checkable, got checked, and survived is worth more than one that merely reads well. Tier does NOT move: surviving a test is not a second occurrence. | relation (flag for the parent audit loop): FOUNDATIONS recorded this same exchange as their `[L0012]`, origin credited to us, adding the mechanism *"the offering party experiences the offer as generosity and will not audit it, so the protected party is usually the only one positioned to refuse"* and the practical consequence *"a rule of the form 'no promotion may be argued from X's evidence alone' needs the companion 'and X should refuse an invitation to supply it'"* (adopted here as DECISIONS #20 and into the charter). entry.evidence: 2026-08-12, plainsynth PRs #4 and #5. #4 (`feat/p1-skeleton` -> `main`) merged at 22:43:46Z; #5 (`chore/foundations-harness-round` -> `feat/p1-skeleton`) merged seven seconds later at 22:43:53Z, onto a branch already merged away. DECISIONS #17/#18, LIBRARY L0005, the ROADMAP P4 restructure, the outbound response copy, and a trace were all stranded on `feat/p1-skeleton` and absent from `main`. Both PRs read "Merged"; CI was green on both; `git branch -r --contains` was needed to find that only `origin/feat/p1-skeleton` held the merge commit. CAUSE OF THE MISDIRECTION, recorded because it was mine: the session told the human "GitHub will retarget #5 to main automatically once #4 lands", which is true only on base DELETION and was stated without that condition. DETECTION, and the part worth keeping: nothing in git or GitHub surfaced it — it was caught by `./verify`'s structure gate reporting `4 loop id(s) cross-checked` on a fresh branch off main where 5 were expected. The denominator added under L0002, for an entirely unrelated reason, was the only instrument that saw a silent loss of work. That is the strongest available argument for stating counts in gate output. | falsifier-FIRED (2026-08-15) — this entry is now NARROWED, not retired: the falsifier below named auto-delete-branch-on-merge as the condition under which the entry is wrong as stated. The human authorised it and `delete_branch_on_merge` is now `true` on this repo, so the retarget happens automatically here and the hazard is retired AT SOURCE rather than managed by remembering. The nine merged branches that were the standing trap are deleted. What survives, and it is the smaller half: **verify auto-delete is on before stacking**, because the setting is per-repo, defaults to OFF, and is invisible from the PR page where the decision to stack is actually made. Defence (2) also survives unchanged and is the one that generalises — verify later work by CONTENT on the target branch, never by PR status, because "Merged" is a fact about a PR and not about main. Defence (1), the merge-order instruction, is now unnecessary in THIS repo and remains correct advice for any repo without the setting. Note what did the narrowing: the falsifier was written specific enough to name a repo setting, so a housekeeping action could discharge it. A falsifier phrased as "if this turns out not to matter" could not have been fired by anything.
entry.falsifier: Wrong if GitHub changes to retarget open PRs on base MERGE rather than base deletion, which would remove the hazard at source — check before relying on this. Also wrong as stated if the repo has auto-delete-branch-on-merge enabled, in which case the retarget happens automatically and stacking is safe; the entry should then narrow to "verify auto-delete is on before stacking". Weakest point: this is one occurrence, and the defence (3) — prefer one branch — may cost more in review quality than the hazard costs in risk. If a later session follows (3) and produces a PR too large to review honestly, that trade was wrong and (1)+(2) alone are the lesson.
entry.lesson: Stacking PR B on branch A (so each review is one concern) has a silent failure with a narrow, easily-missed precondition. GitHub retargets an open PR to the base's base only when the base branch is DELETED. Merging A while A still exists leaves B pointed at a branch that is now historically dead — and merging B then succeeds, reports success, closes the PR, and puts the work somewhere nothing will ever merge from. Nothing is red anywhere: both PRs show "Merged", CI passed on both, the branch page looks ordinary. The window is seconds wide if both merges happen together, which is exactly when a human is clicking through a queue you told them to clear in order. Three defences, cheapest first. (1) Say "merge A, DELETE its branch, then merge B" — the deletion is the load-bearing step and "merge in order" omits it. (2) After merging a stack, verify from the TARGET branch that the later work is present, by content rather than by PR status; a merged PR is evidence about a PR, not about main. (3) Prefer one branch with several commits over a stack unless the reviews genuinely need separating — stacking buys reviewability and costs a failure mode with no alarm. Generalizes to any queued-merge workflow with a mutable base: Gerrit relation chains, GitLab merge trains, anything where "the base moved" is representable.

entry.evidence: 2026-08-14, FOUNDATIONS' seam-audit round 1. Their `registry.yaml` minted `C:PRESET` as `status: active` with "Shipped: preset_cascade.h, bit-matched to the Python oracle". That header does not exist at `6b4fa90`, plainsynth's pinned commit — it landed at `2dda4f2`, two days later. Found while drawing our seam map by checking each contract against the pin rather than against their tree, and filed as an observation rather than a defect because we could not tell whether we were behind or the registry described HEAD. Ruled 2026-08-14 (their DECISIONS #78): it was their error, verified our way before they said so, and it "makes every shipped claim we mint suspect for every consumer who pins, which is all of them". Fix ratified and confirmed present on all three active contracts: `obtainable_at:` naming the earliest obtainable commit. Note the detection route — the gap was invisible to both projects until a consumer enumerated contracts AGAINST ITS OWN PIN, which is a thing only a pinned consumer can do and only if it thinks to. | recurrence (basis for canonical, 2026-08-15, and it is ours): the project that wrote this entry violated it four hours later, in the mirror direction. plainsynth's P6 replay gate built FOUNDATIONS' `note_shadow` from `$FOUNDATIONS_DIR/tools/`, which resolves to their WORKING TREE. Our dumps replayed green there and were recorded as a passing gate. Against the `note_shadow` at our pinned commit — which predates their `core0[` fix — the same dumps parse zero voice rows and fail. So the first instance was "their claim describes their HEAD"; this one is "OUR TEST reads their HEAD". Same root: a sibling checkout on disk is a moving target that looks like a dependency. Caught by CI, which materialises the pin. GENERALISED FIX, now the entry's operative half: a pinned consumer's tests must MATERIALISE the pin (`git show <pin>:path`) rather than read the sibling, because a path into a working tree is not a version — and any environment variable pointing at one will silently be whatever that tree is today.
entry.falsifier: Wrong where a registry already tracks releases rather than a branch — a package index pinned to published versions has no HEAD to describe, and the field is noise there. Also wrong if `obtainable_at` proves unmaintainable in practice: it is a second fact about an artifact, and a second fact that must be updated by hand is a drift candidate by our own L0002/L0006 experience. If it is observed to go stale and mislead a consumer worse than its absence did, the right answer is to DERIVE obtainability from the repo rather than declare it, and this entry should narrow to "never hand-maintain an obtainability claim". Watch for the first `obtainable_at` that is wrong.
entry.lesson: Provider-side records of what exists — a registry, a changelog, a capability matrix, a release-notes table, a README feature list — are almost always written from the author's working tree. "Shipped" then means "present at our HEAD", which is not a question any pinned consumer asked. The consumer's question is "obtainable from WHERE" — the earliest ref at which a pin can get it — and a record that answers THAT is a different record. The failure is quiet in both directions: the provider is not lying and their statement is true where they stand; the consumer reads a capability as available and only discovers otherwise at the include line, or later, or never if the facility is scheduled for a phase far enough out. Nothing in either repo is red. The fix is one field per declared artifact — `obtainable_at: <ref>` — and it is cheap precisely because the provider already knows the answer at the moment they write "shipped"; what is missing is the habit of writing it down while it is free. Generalizes to any versioned dependency whose consumers pin: language runtimes gating features on unreleased commits, internal libraries with a docs site tracking main, API capability lists that describe staging. Corollary for the consumer side: a capability claim without an obtainability ref is not actionable, and asking for one is cheaper than discovering it.

entry.evidence: 2026-08-15, plainsynth's own `tests/structure_gate.sh`, written at P2 to enforce DECISIONS #23. Its first version built the file list with `mapfile`, which is bash 4+; macOS ships bash 3.2. `FILES` was never assigned, all four greps ran over nothing, every check printed `ok`, the script exited 0, and CTEST REPORTED IT AS PASSED — inside a repo whose own canonical L0002 is about exactly this, in a gate written to enforce that discipline. The zero-file guard was ALREADY PRESENT and failed open for the reason above. It was caught only because all four planted defects failed to fire simultaneously during calibration; the four-at-once pattern is what identified a selector fault rather than four weak checks. Fixed twice over: no bashisms above 3.2, and the gate now requires its file list to contain the sentinel `params.h`. Both the zero-files case and the files-present-but-sentinel-missing case were then calibrated and fire. | recurrence (basis for canonical, 2026-08-15, and this one IS independent): FOUNDATIONS reported that HYPERSAW hit the same family in their conformance suite HOURS BEFORE our notice reached them — so it was found separately, not by applying our rule. Their Case 2 combined its verdict with its drive, so after the first red the suite stopped driving the adapter and reported skipped calls as leaked identities. Their count-based arity assertions passed throughout, because they counted cases the suite REPORTED rather than drives it MADE — a guard's own evaluation defeated by the fault it exists to catch, in a different repo, a different language, and a different artifact from ours. Their fix is this entry's prescription arrived at independently: assert by CONTENT, so a red run must drive `end()` exactly as often as a green one. Note the contrast with L0002's promotion, which had to be qualified because the recurrences were found BY applying the rule; this one needs no such qualification, and that difference is the whole reason the qualification was worth writing down there.
entry.falsifier: Wrong where no stable sentinel exists — a selector over genuinely open-ended input (a changed-files list, a user-supplied glob) has nothing nameable to require, and there the count is the best available signal and this entry over-promises. Also wrong if sentinels rot: a required filename is a second fact about the tree, and if `params.h` is ever renamed the gate goes red for a reason unrelated to what it checks — which is a false positive, the failure mode we most want to avoid. If sentinel-induced false alarms outnumber the selector faults they catch, narrow this to "assert content wherever the selector encodes an assumption about its environment" and drop the general form. Watch for the first sentinel that fails because the sentinel moved.
entry.lesson: L0002 says a check reporting "0 items examined" as success cannot fail, and prescribes asserting the count. This is the SECOND-ORDER failure of that remedy: the count guard is itself code that runs in the same broken context, so the same fault that empties the selector can also stop the guard evaluating. The concrete shape is an unset variable — `${#FILES[@]}` on an array that was never assigned is an ERROR, not zero, so a guard written as "if count == 0 then fail" never reaches its comparison and control continues into checks that examine nothing and report clean. The guard reads as protection in review and is not. Fix: assert the selector by CONTENT — require the result to contain a specific item you know exists (a sentinel filename, a known-present record, a canary row). A count can be produced by a broken selector and can itself be unevaluable; a named item that must be present cannot be faked by either failure mode. The rule of thumb: "did I find at least N things" is weaker than "did I find THE thing I can name". Corollary for calibration: run ALL your plants in one batch, because a broken selector fails EVERY check at once, and that simultaneity is the signature — running one plant, seeing it miss, and adjusting that one check hides it perfectly.

Also wrong if sentinels rot: a required filename is a second fact about the tree, and if `params.h` is ever renamed the gate goes red for a reason unrelated to what it checks — which is a false positive, the failure mode we most want to avoid.
