entry.evidence: 2026-08-15, plainsynth P6 (the forensic dump emitter) against FOUNDATIONS' `note.h` at pin `6b4fa90`. `NoteTable` offers eight accessors taking a `NoteHandle` — bind, slot, retarget, unbind, boundCount, state, live, end — and NONE returns the `NoteRef` non-destructively; `end()` returns it and frees the row, `noteOn()` returns `stolen` having already displaced it, and `forEachMatch` yields handles rather than refs. Their own `note_shadow` never hits this because it BUILDS a table from parsed events and only needs `state()`. Our emitter needs the opposite direction and recovers identities by a 128-key wildcard scan, with the result compared against `activeCount()` so a key outside the MIDI range reports `complete: false` instead of vanishing. The alternative was a parallel identity copy, declined because duplicated state is the drift the type exists to prevent. Filed as DECISIONS #27; may well be deliberate (handing out identities invites caching them past their generation), in which case the finding is that the header does not say so. | corroboration (2026-08-15, and deliberately NOT a promotion): FOUNDATIONS ruled the missing accessor a real gap rather than a deliberate refusal, declining the refusal argument we had constructed for them, and reported that THREE parties hit it — us as a producer, HYPERSAW writing a conformance adapter, and the library's own author writing a gate-off fixture, who reached for the accessor, found none, and built the parallel tag table we had declined. The third is the strongest support for this entry's MECHANISM: when the authors themselves moved into the producing direction, they hit the same wall their consuming tools never touch. TIER UNCHANGED, because the falsifier below asks for a second instance in a DIFFERENT LIBRARY and all three hits are the same gap in the same type. Three parties proving one gap is real is not three instances of a pattern, and conflating them is precisely the arithmetic L0004 is about.
entry.falsifier: Wrong if this is an ordinary one-off omission rather than a directional pattern — one missing accessor in one type proves a gap, not a rule. It needs a second instance in a different library before the "authors' unused direction" framing earns anything, and if the next few gaps we hit are randomly distributed across directions, this is pattern-matching on one data point and should be demoted. Also wrong if the omission turns out to be a deliberate refusal that a consumer SHOULD respect — if FOUNDATIONS rules that identities are intentionally unreadable from handles to prevent caching, then the correct lesson is much narrower ("expect deliberate refusals to look like gaps, and ask before working around one") and this entry should be rewritten to that.
entry.lesson: A library type usually gets used in one direction by the people who wrote it, and the accessors follow that use. The reverse direction — same data, opposite question — is where the missing method is, and its absence is invisible from inside because the authors' own tests and tools never ask it. The tell is asymmetry in the accessor set: a type that lets you SET or MATCH on a field but never READ it back from the handle you were given. Concretely, a consumer that BUILDS state from an event stream needs only "what state is this in"; a producer that REPORTS state needs "who is this" — and a table designed by consumers will have `state(h)` and no `identity(h)`. The practical damage is not the missing call, it is the two bad options it forces: recover the value by SEARCH (expensive, and bounded searches silently miss out-of-range values), or keep a PARALLEL COPY of the data the library already holds — which is exactly the duplication such libraries usually exist to eliminate, reintroduced by the library's own gap. Corollary for anyone integrating: the highest-value thing a new consumer can do early is USE THE SEAM IN A DIRECTION ITS AUTHORS DO NOT, because that is the only direction where "it fits" is not a foregone conclusion. Where a scan is unavoidable, compare its result against a count the library reports and declare incompleteness rather than emitting something that looks whole.

entry.evidence: 2026-08-15, plainsynth P7 against FOUNDATIONS' `mod_routing.h`. `EndpointKind::kParam`'s comment read "a registry parameter (ParamAddress)", so we concluded that a modulation source must be a host-facing registry entry, that our envelope and velocity sources therefore had no expressible kind, and we filed a brief recording the routing half of P7 as BLOCKED. It was not: `mod_routing.h` does not include `registry.h` and never had, and the endpoint check is `address.valid()` and nothing more. A two-line probe — one routing from an unregistered address, `-fsyntax-only` — settled it in under a minute AFTER the ruling came back. Cost: half a phase. THREE comment defects have now been found in that one provider's headers (`kLeafShadowsAncestor` narrower than its check in both directions; `kParam` inventing a constraint; `scope_selector` asserting a semantics the same file calls uninterpreted) and in all three the code was correct. Their framing, adopted: for a doorframe, the comments are most of the interface, so a wrong comment is a wrong doorframe. Ours, which they adopted in return: our comment was wrong and our verification was missing, and BOTH had to hold for the block to exist.
entry.falsifier: Wrong where the constraint is genuinely unprobeable — a runtime licence check, a rate limit, a "do not call this on the audio thread" rule whose violation is a data race rather than a compile error. There the comment is the only signal and this entry offers nothing. Also wrong if probing becomes a habit that erodes trust usefully placed: a consumer who tests every documented statement burns time on the 95% that are accurate, and the discipline should stay attached to constraints that BLOCK, not to descriptions. Narrow it to that if the probes start costing more than the one block they saved. Watch for the first probe that wastes an afternoon confirming something true.
entry.lesson: A provider's header comments are read as the interface and tested as nothing. The code has compilers, tests and consumers hammering it; the prose beside it has one author and one review, and it drifts the moment behaviour changes without it. So a comment stating a CONSTRAINT — "X must be registered", "Y means global", "Z is not permitted" — is a claim with no verifier behind it, and treating it as a fact is how a consumer becomes blocked by a rule that does not exist. The cheap countermeasure is asymmetric in your favour: a constraint you have only READ can usually be tested in a couple of lines and a `-fsyntax-only` pass, so run it BEFORE you record yourself blocked, redesign around it, or file it. Doing so converts "we are blocked" into either "we are blocked and here is the compiler saying so" or "your comment is wrong", and the second is worth far more to both sides. The effect is strongest where the artifact is mostly prose BY CONSTRUCTION — a declaration-only header, a doorframe, an interface spec that evaluates nothing — because there the comments ARE most of the interface and the code cannot contradict them loudly enough to keep them honest. Corollary, and it is the harder half: the probe is most necessary exactly when the constraint sounds authoritative, since that is when you will not think to run it.

entry.evidence: 2026-08-15 — spawn of the venv python from an identically-flagged node ran server.py up to bind(); the same build's existsSync(cfg.python) failed live in Live with the restricted-API error, masquerading as a bad config. Removing the pre-flight made auto-start work first try.
entry.falsifier: a future SDK/host loosens or documents the allowlist, or Node's permission model starts propagating to spawned children.
entry.lesson: The Extension Host runs Node with `--permission --allow-child-process --allow-fs-read=<Extensions dir> --allow-fs-read=<Extensions Data dir> --allow-fs-write=<Extensions Data dir>`. Two consequences that pull in opposite directions: (a) `child_process.spawn` of an interpreter anywhere on disk WORKS — the permission model does not propagate to the child; but (b) any Node fs call on a path outside the allowlist (`existsSync`, `readFileSync` on `~/Documents/...`) throws "Access to this API has been restricted. Use --allow-fs-read to manage permissions." So do not "helpfully" pre-check a path you are about to spawn — let spawn's ENOENT tell you. The only extension-writable location is `environment.storageDirectory` (under Extensions Data); machine-local config belongs there.
entry.title: The host's fs sandbox binds Node, not the children Node spawns

entry.evidence: 2026-08-11 — spent a cycle reading b10's log showing "4 MidiClip actions" while the running host wrote to b11; `ls -dt` ranked b7 first by mtime.
entry.falsifier: the SDK/CLI gains a documented way to query the active log path, or Live stops version-stamping the preferences directory.
entry.lesson: The host log lives in a **version-stamped** directory (`~/Library/Preferences/Ableton/Live <ver>/ExtensionHost.txt`), and a beta update silently moves it — Live went 12.4.5b10 → b11 mid-session here. Picking the directory by newest mtime (`ls -dt`) is wrong twice over: an old version's folder can be touched more recently than the live one (b7 sorted first while b11 was in use), so you end up reading a stale log and concluding the extension did not load, or that an old build is still installed. Resolve it from the running process instead: `ps aux | grep -o "logFilePath':'[^']*'"` — the host is launched with its log path as an argument, so this is authoritative.
entry.supersedes_note: (sharpens L0005's diagnostic order: step 0 is "am I even reading the right log?")
